implementation_notes: Scala exposes CPS directly through scala.util.control.TailCalls: a @tailrec method returns TailCall[T], each of which holds the next step, and the generated trampoline in scala.util.control.TailCalls\$.run executes them in constant stack space. This is the library form of CPS plus trampolining, and it exists because the JVM has no tail-call elimination. For genuinely stackless continuations, cats-free code often uses Either or a hand-rolled State monad, which is CPS with a monadic wrapper. Scala also has delimited continuations (scala.util.continuations) in the standard library for exactly this shape.
idiom_name: scala.util.control.TailCalls (@tailrec + trampoline); delimited continuations in scala.util.continuations
pitfalls: @tailrec on a method whose recursive call is not in tail position is a compile error, not a warning - the annotation is a proof obligation.
A TailCall built by hand and returned from a non-tail position reintroduces the stack growth the trampoline removed.
Continuations in a loop that re-enter shift accumulate the delimited context; and/orElse-style biasing matters when both branches are tried.
